transcript:
-- Meeting Header --
Date: 2026-06-18
Start time: 16:30 PDT
Duration: 57 minutes
Meeting ID: rwd-20260618-128k-pd-001
Attendees: Isabel Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Karthik Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, Helix), Ben Torres (ML Eng), Priya Nair (Platform), Samir Gupta (Security)

Summary: Technical deep dive on long-context (128k+) runtime performance. Covered batching strategies, KV cache behavior, eviction, attention optimizations, chunking/overlap tradeoffs, and deployment options (Dedicated vs Private/VPC). Agreed on next steps: run a customer benchmark, share security docs and pricing, and provide chunking examples.

Topics: 128k context performance, continuous batching, KV cache eviction policy, quantization impact on throughput, VPC/on-prem constraints, kernel selection, SLA/latency SLOs.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Isabel Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, quick round of intros? We have Marco and Karthik from Redwood who will cover the heavy runtime details.
[00:10] Aisha Khan: Hi, Aisha here, CTO at Helix. Ben is on for ML infra and Priya for platform. Samir from security is also on.
[00:16] Marco Ruiz: Great. Scope for today: long context, 128k plus, uh, how we get latency and throughput to look reasonable, and practical chunking patterns. We'll try to keep it technical.
[00:26] Ben Torres: Quick context from our side — we ingest multi-megabyte regulatory documents. Our goal is to do few-shot summarization and entity extraction across whole content, ideally with single-session context. Latency target in prod: p95 < 800ms for a 4k token response; we under-stand cost is a factor.
[00:44] Karthik Patel: Thanks. Couple quick clarifying questions: what's your average sequence length incoming, and do you expect streaming partial outputs or final batch outputs?
[00:52] Priya Nair: Avg doc size is 60-200k tokens after tokenization across sections, we typically chunk at ingestion. We want streaming for user experience but can tolerate small buffering.
[01:05] Marco Ruiz: Ok. On 128k+ workflows, there are two main approaches we recommend: 1) full long-context runtime with optimized attention + KV cache and chunked attention kernels (we refer to Atlas-128k profile internally), or 2) chunk-and-stitch: break into overlapping chunks, run shorter-context models and stitch results. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:26] Ben Torres: Can you be specific on tradeoffs? latency/throughput numbers?
[01:29] Marco Ruiz: Sure — rough numbers, depends on hardware. On a 4xA100-like Dedicated node, using our long-context execution path with kv-sparse attention kernels and block attention, we see token throughput of ~14-18 tokens/sec for 128k context for generation with quantized FP16 kernels. Latency for the first token often dominated by KV warm-up; subsequent tokens are faster. For chunk-and-stitch with a 16k model, we can hit 60-80 tokens/sec but you pay overhead re-encoding and stitching, and some cross-chunk understanding is lost unless you do overlap and attention pooling which increases cost. (transcription: numbers approximate)
[02:12] Aisha Khan: Those throughput numbers seem low vs our SLA — we need p95 under 800ms for responses of a few thousand tokens. How do you get there?
[02:20] Marco Ruiz: Two levers: latency-focused routing + batching config. For interactive SLOs we put requests on latency optimized pools (lower batch sizes, reserved heads), use prefix caching aggressively — if users are mostly reading same docs, the KV cache prevents re-decoding of prefix tokens. Also kernel selection: fused attention kernels + rotary embedding caching help.
[02:41] Samir Gupta: How deterministic is the KV cache? We have compliance concerns—if a user deletes data we need to ensure eviction and auditability.
[02:49] Karthik Patel: Good question. Our KV cache supports TTL and explicit eviction APIs. We log cache writes and evictions to the audit trail. For Private/VPC deployments you control the KMS and audit retention. There's a small eventual consistency window if you run distributed cache shards but we can pin single-tenant shards in Dedicated.
[03:10] Ben Torres: I want to understand memory behavior. 128k context seems massive for KV storage — what are the memory footprints?
[03:18] Marco Ruiz: Rough ballpark: per token KV in FP16 ~ 8 bytes per entry per head times number of heads and layers; for a 70B class model with 64 heads and 32 layers, it's... the math gets big quickly — which is why we do compression and chunked KV frames. In practice, our runtime keeps active working sets in GPU memory and spills cold segments to host memory. For Helix we recommend Dedicated nodes with 4x48GB GPUs or higher with NVMe spill for that working set. Quantization down to 4-bit for weights helps throughput but doesn't reduce KV size much because KV cache is activation-level precision; we use half-precision for KV to avoid quality drops.
[04:05] Priya Nair: So quantization helps model weights but not KV? That impacts our cost model.
[04:10] Karthik Patel: Right — quantization reduces model memory and increases kernel speed but KV cache remains FP16 often. Some experimental pathways store KV in 8-bit with a small degration; we can test that in a PoC.
[04:23] Aisha Khan: About chunking strategies — can you show a recommended pattern? Sliding window size and overlap?
[04:30] Marco Ruiz: Typical for extraction/QA: chunk length 8k-16k with 10-20% overlap for context continuity. For summarization of long docs we sometimes do hierarchical chunking: 1) chunk 16k -> produce chunk summaries; 2) combine summaries into a 64k concatenation -> final pass. That reduces runtime while preserving coherence. We'll send sample scripts.
[04:53] Ben Torres: If we pick the full 128k runtime, what's the impact on concurrency?
[04:58] Marco Ruiz: Concurrency drops because each request uses larger working sets; effective concurrent requests per node is lower. That's where Dedicated pools and autoscaling come in: reserve capacity for predictable burst. For strict low-latency we recommend a hybrid: latency pool runs smaller-context models for interactive flows and falls back to 128k workers for async batch jobs.
[05:18] Samir Gupta: Network/VPC question: for Private deployment, how does peering work? We need no open ingress from internet and should route via private peering.
[05:27] Karthik Patel: For Private we support VPC peering and direct connect. Our control plane can be customer-managed in VPC; compute can be in your account for on-prem. We'll provide firewall rule template and guidance — typical pattern is establish peering, expose only internal load balancer, and use mTLS + SAML SSO.
[05:45] Priya Nair: Any differences for on-prem in terms of kernel availability? Our hardware is a mix of H100 and A100.
[05:51] Marco Ruiz: Kernels are selected at runtime. H100 tends to do better on fp8 and newer attention kernels; A100 has maturity for existing fp16 paths. We tune compilation flags per device. We'll provide a recommended config mapping for H100 vs A100.
[06:06] Ben Torres: Can you talk about batching strategies — continuous batching vs fixed windows?
[06:11] Marco Ruiz: Continuous batching is our default in hosted and Dedicated: small requests are aggregated into token-aware batches; we balance latency by having a max-accumulate time (e.g., 8-12ms) and max batch size. For 128k context workloads, batch sizing is tricky because memory constrains batch depth — we do dynamic batch shaping where we prefer more tokens at lower sequence lengths; long queries may be processed with smaller batch sizes.
[06:35] Aisha Khan: Any guidance on SLOs we should set for PoC to validate performance?
[06:39] Isabel Chen: Recommend two SLOs: Latency SLO (p95 < 1s for interactive X token responses) and Throughput SLO (sustained N tokens/sec per node). We'll help define the exact numbers during benchmark.
[06:51] Ben Torres: Could you run a benchmark on our sample corpus? We've uploaded 50 doc examples to the dropbox link in the invite.
[06:58] Marco Ruiz: Yes — Marco will run two benchmarks: 1) full long-context (128k exec path) on Dedicated-like hardware; 2) chunk-and-stitch using 16k windows with overlap. We'll report latency distributions, memory/CPU/GPU telemetry, and cost estimates.
[07:12] Samir Gupta: About audit logs for cache evictions and token-level events — how granular are logs and how long can they be retained?
[07:19] Karthik Patel: We log cache writes/reads/evictions with token offsets and associated request IDs; retention is configurable in Private and Dedicated (we offer 90/365/730 day tiers). For hosted, we have standard retention windows but can support enterprise retention via add-on. We'll include a sample audit schema in the security pack.
[07:36] Aisha Khan: There was concern internally about hallucination when combining chunked outputs. Do you have recommended evals?
[07:43] Marco Ruiz: Yes — we recommend prompt-level evals and overlap-consistency tests: compute n-gram overlap and factual consistency across overlapping windows, and set a regression threshold. Our Optimize tooling can monitor quality and raise regression alerts.
[07:58] Ben Torres: Any mention of competitors doing long-context better?
[08:01] Isabel Chen: A few customers asked about Anthropic and OpenAI approaches; we discussed tradeoffs earlier. We'll send a short comparison doc.
[08:10] Priya Nair: Ok practical steps — timeline for PoC and security review?
[08:14] Isabel Chen: PoC run next week; security review parallel. We'll aim to have initial benchmark results by 2026-06-25.
[08:20] Marco Ruiz: Quick caveat on numbers — real perf will depend on prompt shapes and tokenization quirks; sometimes proper nouns get tokenized weird and change the lengths.
[08:28] Ben Torres: Noted. Also curious about model variants: if we quantize weights to 4-bit for cost, do you see large regressions on extraction tasks?
[08:36] Karthik Patel: For many extraction tasks 4-bit quantization with per-channel scales is acceptable; for fine-grained NER we saw minor accuracy drops in internal tests. We recommend A/Bing the quantized profile in the PoC.
[08:49] Samir Gupta: Encryption key management question — for Private, can we bring our own HSM?
[08:54] Marco Ruiz: Yes, BYOK is supported for Private deployment and Dedicated with enterprise contract. We'll include KMS integration notes.
[09:02] Aisha Khan: Anything else on operational tooling?
[09:06] Karthik Patel: Observability: token-level traces, per-route latency, KV cache hitrates, and per-model cost breakdowns. You can set cost alerts per-route.
[09:18] Ben Torres: What's the expected work to set up VPC peering and a PoC? We have infra team availability next week.
[09:24] Isabel Chen: Typically 1-2 days of infra work to set up peering and firewall rules and another day to validate endpoints. We'll provide a checklist.
[09:33] Marco Ruiz: Ok we'll summarize config: 1) choose Dedicated node type (we recommend 4xA100 80GB or H100 for faster long-context), 2) enable KV pinning and NVMe spill, 3) tune continuous batching max-accumulate to 10ms for interactive flows, 4) enable prefix caching with TTL 24-72 hours depending on change rate.
[09:56] Priya Nair: Will you include estimated node counts for our expected load of ~100 concurrent users?
[10:01] Marco Ruiz: We'll include that in the benchmark report — preliminary guess: if we prioritize latency with hybrid pools maybe 3-6 Dedicated nodes depending on request shapes.
[10:10] Aisha Khan: Great. Let's move to recap and owners.
[10:13] Isabel Chen: Recap: Marco and Karthik run benchmarks (128k execution path + chunk-and-stitch) on Helix dataset; Marco/Karthik provide chunking scripts and kernel configs; Isabel sends pricing and contract notes; Karthik sends security pack. Samir will share network contact.
[10:28] Ben Torres: One minor nit — can you include an example of the sliding window code in Python?
[10:32] Karthik Patel: Yes we'll attach sample script and a quickstart repo link.
[10:36] Aisha Khan: Ok good. Thanks everyone.
[10:39] Isabel Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and calendar invite for the review.
[10:44] Samir Gupta: Thanks.
